name: Wendy Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we aren't selling anything. What you say is confidential, so you can tell me your public line and what you think privately. What does a normal day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Wendy, 27, and I lead a small maintenance team at a tech company. I studied for a master's, and I like tracing a payment fault all the way to the line that caused it; then I review the fix before release. Meetings about new tools wear me out because someone always wants speed without checking a customer's bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my team the grand promises ran ahead of the actual tools. A script that sorts our bug reports is useful, but it doesn't design a safe release.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could live with that, except our little company already pays me below what a lead developer ought to earn. I have three weeks of rent and food saved, and there are hardly any software teams close enough to commute to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep reviewing the payment code by hand and ask for the promised pay review in January. If the small tools save time, fine, but I won't put customer records into one or pretend a shortcut is a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly tired, honestly. The AI noise would quiet down, but the pay problem would still be on my kitchen table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which expense is already hard to cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rent takes nearly half my pay. I stopped visiting my sister on weekends because the train fare added up, and that was before any of these pictures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound confident in your skill but worried about cash; how do those fit together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know I sound stubborn. I earned a master's degree and led the last migration, so asking for a fair rate is not refusing change.

say: I'd say the **bug sorter** helps, but people still own the release.
I'd tell colleagues the **grand promises** were too big.
think: I worry more about **low pay** and three weeks of savings than AI.
My **lead work** deserves a better rate, even if I dislike new tools.
do: Keep **manual review** of payment code through the first year.
Ask for the **January pay review** my manager promised.
feel: **Tired** from the rent pressure, with some relief that work stays familiar.
S0.quote: The AI noise would quiet down, but the pay problem would still be on my kitchen table.
fieldNote: **Rent pressure** predates AI and drives her mood even under the mild card.
She links **professional pride** to careful code review, not to rejecting every small tool.

steps.text: Keep reviewing payment releases by hand through the first year
Ask the manager for the promised January pay review

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we should test what the coding tools actually get right. I wouldn't be the one cheering when a junior seat disappears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Private truth? Our firm sells software maintenance, and writing fixes and checking tests take most of my week. If software does those tasks cheaply, management could keep one lead and stop hiring juniors, then ask the lead to cover twice as much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the developers' association meetings with the junior staff and ask the group to seek a written list of tasks moving to software. I would redirect 60 a month from takeaway meals into savings while the first changes roll in; I won't use an AI coding tool on live code without a checked trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy would be too mild. I can picture the support queue getting shorter while my workload and the chance of a cut both grow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Whose place is most exposed when fewer people are hired?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nadia, our newest developer, catches mistakes in customer wording that I miss. If her place is cut, we lose her eye for customer confusion. The company may save one salary and lose the pair of eyes that knows when a customer is confused.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever try the tool yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try a contained trial if the firm gave us test data and time to check it. I don't want customer payment details fed into a tool merely to hit a faster target.

say: I'd ask for **tested results** before changing how we release software.
I'd object if the firm removed a **junior seat** without discussing the work left behind.
think: I spend **most of my week** on routine fixes and tests, so my hours may be at risk.
I fear a thinner team could leave me with **more work** and less security.
do: Attend **developers' association** meetings and seek a joint written task request.
Redirect **60 monthly** from takeaway meals into savings if my budget allows it.
S1.quote: The company may save one salary and lose the pair of eyes that knows when a customer is confused.
fieldNote: **Code and tests** dominate her work, making steady change personally threatening.
Her public call for **testing** hides a fear that management could both cut staff and stretch her hours.

steps.text: Ask the developers' association to request a written task list
Attend developers' association meetings with junior colleagues
Redirect 60 monthly from takeaway meals into savings if affordable

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say no employer should promise secure jobs it can't back up. Full thinking AI by 2028 would reach our code long before those 2031 robots matter to a software team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my role could go quickly. My master's and the fact I lead releases might buy months, but a cheap system that writes and checks code would strike the thing my wage is for. Three weeks of savings is not a bridge to another career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd get the mortgage-free spare room my aunt offered priced properly, because I might need to leave my flat. In the first year after 2028, if my hours are cut, I'd move there and apply for technician apprenticeships with the local repair firms; I'd also ask the association to push for paid training before cuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm frightened. I'd probably keep sounding firm at work, then lie awake counting rent days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the spare-room offer exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My aunt has said I could stay for six months and pay towards bills, not live there for free forever. I'd check that offer with her before making it my plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you keep to yourself at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't tell my team that I have no answer ready. I'd tell them I need a little time to put a real one together.

say: I'd say **2028 thinking AI** reaches our code before robots arrive around 2031.
I'd ask employers for **honest job promises** and paid training.
think: I fear cheap code writing and checking could erase **my lead role** quickly.
I cannot fund a **career change** with three weeks of savings alone.
do: Check **my aunt's room** and six-month terms now; move there if coding hours fall after 2028.
Apply for **repair apprenticeships** if hours fall in the first year after 2028.
Push through the **association** for employer-funded training before cuts.
feel: **Frightened** enough to count rent days at night.
S2.quote: Three weeks of savings is not a bridge to another career.
fieldNote: **2028 code automation** would hit her work directly; later robots offer no breathing room.
Her **aunt's room** is conditional and temporary, so it cannot erase the cash shock.

steps.text: Check six-month room and bill terms with her aunt
Move into her aunt's room for six months at most if coding hours are cut
Apply to local repair technician apprenticeships after a cut
Ask the developers' association to press for paid training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives firms time to be honest about where coding work goes. The robots coming around 2034 don't change that software jobs face the 2031 thinking system first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might have enough time to leave on my own terms, if I act rather than wait for my title to save me. My savings are still thin, though, and a training place would have to be paid or I couldn't take it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter I'd visit two electronics repair shops and ask what their apprentices actually earn. If one offers a paid place that covers rent, I'd enroll before 2031; in the first year after the thinking AI arrives, I'd keep the software job only while it still pays and finish the practical training. I wouldn't buy a house on a forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious, but I can make a calendar instead of just counting days. I don't trust the calendar to protect everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What sort of other work would you ask about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I mean real bench work, fault finding and replacing parts, not another desk job with a new title. Robots may change that work around 2034, so I would ask the shops how their repair work is changing before signing anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your family say about leaving software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents would tell me to keep the steady wage. I'd show my parents the pay figures and let them argue with the numbers, not with a headline.

say: I'd ask firms for a **2031 staffing plan** while there is time.
I'd say **2034 robots** are a later question for repair work.
think: My **lead title** may not protect coding income when thinking AI arrives.
I need a **paid training place** that covers rent before I can change course.
do: Visit **two repair shops** this winter to check apprentice pay.
Enroll before 2031 only if a **paid place** covers rent.
Keep the **software wage** during the first year after 2031 while finishing training.
feel: **Anxious**, though five years allows a practical calendar.
S3.quote: I'd show my parents the pay figures and let them argue with the numbers, not with a headline.
fieldNote: **Five years** turns fear into a conditional plan with pay figures.
She knows **repair robots** could follow around 2034 and asks before moving into that trade.

steps.text: Enroll in paid repair training only if wages cover rent
Keep software wages while finishing practical training after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues a decade lets us make choices instead of taking whatever comes. Coding still faces the 2036 thinking AI; waiting for the 2039 robots would be a mistake for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 37 I could have a different career and a better cushion, but I cannot assume either happens. I can also imagine staying in software if customers still want a person accountable for releases; that is a question, not a guarantee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd first ask for the pay review and build three months of expenses before paying for any course. Over the decade I'd test repair training on weekends if the price is modest, and in the first year after 2036 I'd choose between release oversight and repair work based on actual paid offers. I would not borrow heavily to chase a prediction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cautious, and a bit relieved by the time. Rent still makes me anxious, and I know the end point hasn't softened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a newer developer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell a younger developer to keep a record of the faults they solved and the clients who trusted them. A course certificate alone would not pay a younger developer's rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a course worth paying for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My line would be simple: show me the wages and the hours. If the offer is real, I'll change; if not, I still need to eat next month.

say: I'd say **2036 thinking AI** reaches coding years before 2039 robots.
I'd ask colleagues to keep **records of solved faults** and trusted clients.
think: I could build a **better cushion** over a decade, but nothing guarantees it.
I might still earn from release oversight if **clients pay** for a person to own errors.
do: Build **three months' expenses** before buying training.
Try **weekend repair training** if the cost stays modest.
Compare **paid offers** for release oversight and repair in the year after 2036.
feel: **Anxious** about rent, though ten years gives me time to do the sums.
S4.quote: A course certificate alone would not pay a younger developer's rent.
fieldNote: **Ten years** gives room to save and test a trade without borrowing heavily.
She makes her later choice depend on **paid offers**, not a prediction about human oversight.

steps.text: Save three months of expenses before paying for a course
Try modestly priced weekend electronics repair training
Compare paid release oversight and repair offers after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. Paid training before a cut, and an honest list of which jobs remain, would give me something I can act on; vague assurances won't cover the rent.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask why a team lead has so little put away. I paid for the last part of my master's while taking a lower paid lead role near my family, and the rent rose. Being good at the job hasn't made me rich.

headlineQuote: Being good at the job hasn't made me rich.
portrait: At **27**, Wendy leads software maintenance and reviews payment releases after earning a master's degree.
Her **lower pay** and rising rent leave less than one month saved, despite strong technical skill.
She avoids AI tools, trusts **checked releases**, and asks for fair pay under AI Plateau.
Steady change threatens **coding hours**; fast AGI frightens her, while five years allows conditional paid repair training.
With ten years, she would build **savings** and compare real paid offers before leaving software.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her coding income before she can afford another trade.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training** before cuts and a clear list of remaining jobs would let her plan.
